faq.question: What is endometriosis?
faq.answer: Endometriosis is a chronic, estrogen-dependent inflammatory condition in which tissue similar to the endometrium (the inner lining of the uterus) grows outside the uterus. These implants most commonly occur on the ovaries, fallopian tubes, outer surface of the uterus, and the peritoneum (pelvic lining), but can also affect the bowel, bladder, rectum, and in rare cases, distant organs such as the lungs or diaphragm. Like normal endometrial tissue, these implants respond to hormonal changes during the menstrual cycle — thickening, breaking down, and bleeding — but the blood has no way to exit the body, leading to inflammation, scarring, and adhesions.

faq.question: What causes endometriosis?
faq.answer: The exact cause of endometriosis is not fully understood. Several theories exist: (1) Retrograde menstruation (Sampson's theory) — menstrual blood flows backward through the fallopian tubes into the pelvic cavity, implanting endometrial cells on pelvic organs; this is the most widely accepted theory but does not explain all cases; (2) Coelomic metaplasia — peritoneal cells transform into endometrial-like cells under hormonal or immune triggers; (3) Lymphatic or vascular spread — explains rare distant implants (e.g., lungs, brain); (4) Immune dysfunction — impaired immune surveillance fails to clear ectopic endometrial cells; (5) Genetic predisposition — first-degree relatives have a 7-10 times higher risk. Endometriosis is likely the result of a combination of these mechanisms.

faq.question: What are the symptoms of endometriosis?
faq.answer: Endometriosis presents with a wide range of symptoms, and severity does not always correlate with the extent of disease. Common symptoms include: dysmenorrhea (painful periods, often severe and progressively worsening); chronic pelvic pain (non-cyclic, persisting beyond menstruation); dyspareunia (deep pain during or after sexual intercourse); dyschezia (painful bowel movements, especially during menstruation); dysuria (painful urination during menstruation); heavy menstrual bleeding or irregular bleeding; bloating (endometriosis belly); infertility; and fatigue. Up to 25% of women with endometriosis are asymptomatic, with the condition discovered incidentally during surgery or fertility investigations.

faq.question: How is endometriosis diagnosed?
faq.answer: Definitive diagnosis of endometriosis requires surgical visualization, typically by laparoscopy, with histological confirmation of biopsy specimens showing endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus. However, clinical diagnosis based on symptoms, physical examination, and imaging is increasingly accepted to allow earlier treatment without surgery. Transvaginal ultrasound is the first-line imaging investigation — it is highly accurate for detecting ovarian endometriomas and deep infiltrating endometriosis involving the rectovaginal septum and bladder. MRI provides superior soft-tissue detail for deep infiltrating disease and surgical planning. CA-125 is non-specific and not recommended as a diagnostic test.

faq.question: How long does it take to diagnose endometriosis?
faq.answer: The average diagnostic delay for endometriosis is 7-10 years from symptom onset to confirmed diagnosis. This delay occurs because: symptoms such as painful periods are often normalized or dismissed; symptoms overlap with other conditions (irritable bowel syndrome, pelvic inflammatory disease, ovarian cysts); awareness among patients and clinicians is historically low; and definitive diagnosis traditionally required surgery. Early recognition of classic symptoms (progressive dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia, cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms) combined with clinical examination and ultrasound can allow empirical treatment to begin without waiting for surgical confirmation.

faq.question: What are the stages of endometriosis?
faq.answer: Endometriosis is classified into four stages by the American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) revised classification based on the location, extent, and depth of implants, ovarian involvement, and degree of adhesions: Stage I (Minimal) — isolated superficial implants, no significant adhesions; Stage II (Mild) — superficial and some deep implants, minor adhesions; Stage III (Moderate) — multiple deep implants, small endometriomas on one or both ovaries, filmy adhesions; Stage IV (Severe) — large endometriomas, extensive dense adhesions, severe distortion of pelvic anatomy. Importantly, symptom severity and fertility impact do not reliably correlate with surgical stage — minimal disease can cause severe pain, while extensive disease may be asymptomatic.

faq.question: What is an endometrioma?
faq.answer: An endometrioma, also called a 'chocolate cyst', is a type of ovarian cyst formed when endometriosis tissue invades the ovary, creating a cyst filled with old, dark brown menstrual blood. Endometriomas occur in approximately 17-44% of women with endometriosis. They can cause pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and reduced ovarian reserve (diminished egg supply). On ultrasound, they appear as homogeneous low-level internal echoes ('ground glass'). Treatment options include hormonal suppression (COCPs, GnRH agonists) to prevent growth, or laparoscopic cystectomy (surgical removal). Cystectomy improves pain and spontaneous conception rates but may further reduce ovarian reserve, so careful consideration is needed in women planning fertility treatment.

faq.question: What is deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE)?
faq.answer: Deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE) is the most severe form of endometriosis, defined as endometriotic lesions penetrating more than 5mm beneath the peritoneal surface. It commonly affects the uterosacral ligaments, rectovaginal septum, bowel (rectum, sigmoid colon), bladder, and ureters. DIE causes the most severe symptoms including debilitating dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia, cyclical rectal bleeding or diarrhea, urinary urgency and hematuria, and severe chronic pelvic pain. Diagnosis requires MRI or expert transvaginal ultrasound with bowel preparation. Surgical treatment of DIE is complex, often requiring multidisciplinary teams including colorectal and urological surgeons.

faq.question: How does endometriosis affect fertility?
faq.answer: Endometriosis affects fertility through multiple mechanisms: distortion of pelvic anatomy and adhesions that block the fallopian tubes or impair ovum pick-up; endometriomas reducing ovarian reserve and egg quality; inflammatory mediators in the peritoneal fluid impairing sperm function and embryo implantation; and altered endometrial receptivity. Approximately 30-50% of women with endometriosis experience infertility. However, many women with endometriosis conceive naturally or with assistance. Treatment options include laparoscopic surgery to remove implants and adhesions (improves spontaneous pregnancy rates in mild-moderate disease), ovulation induction, intrauterine insemination (IUI), and IVF (most effective for severe disease or tubal factor).

faq.question: What are the treatment options for endometriosis?
faq.answer: Endometriosis treatment is individualized based on symptom severity, location of disease, desire for fertility, and patient preference. Options include: (1) Analgesia — NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) for pain relief; (2) Hormonal suppression — combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs), progestins (norethisterone, dienogest), levonorgestrel IUS (Mirena), GnRH agonists (leuprolide, goserelin) with add-back therapy, or GnRH antagonists (elagolix); (3) Surgical treatment — laparoscopic excision or ablation of implants, adhesiolysis, cystectomy for endometriomas, or hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for severe refractory disease; (4) Multidisciplinary pain management — physiotherapy, psychology, pain specialists, dietitian. Hormonal treatments suppress but do not cure endometriosis; recurrence after stopping treatment is common.

faq.question: What is the role of hormonal therapy in endometriosis?
faq.answer: Hormonal therapy works by suppressing estrogen production or opposing its effects, thereby reducing the growth and activity of endometriotic implants and relieving pain. Options include: combined oral contraceptive pills (first-line; suppress ovulation and reduce menstrual flow); progestins such as dienogest (highly effective for pain; first-line medical treatment in many guidelines); the levonorgestrel IUS (Mirena; particularly effective for dysmenorrhea and heavy bleeding); GnRH agonists (leuprolide, goserelin, nafarelin; highly effective but cause menopausal side effects; add-back HRT minimizes bone loss and vasomotor symptoms); and GnRH antagonists (elagolix; newer oral option with more flexible dosing). None of these treatments cure endometriosis, and symptoms typically recur after stopping therapy.

faq.question: Is surgery necessary for endometriosis?
faq.answer: Surgery is not always necessary and depends on symptom severity, response to medical treatment, and fertility goals. Laparoscopy is indicated when: diagnosis needs confirmation; symptoms are severe and not controlled by hormonal therapy or analgesics; endometriomas are present (particularly > 4cm); deep infiltrating endometriosis causes significant bowel, bladder, or ureteral involvement; or fertility is affected. Laparoscopic excision (cutting out lesions) is superior to ablation (burning) for pain relief and fertility outcomes. Hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is a last resort for severe refractory disease in women who have completed their family, but is not guaranteed to eliminate all symptoms if implants remain.

faq.question: Can endometriosis be cured?
faq.answer: There is currently no cure for endometriosis. Even after surgical removal of all visible lesions, recurrence rates are significant — approximately 20-30% within 2 years and up to 50% within 5 years without ongoing hormonal suppression. Hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy (removal of uterus and both ovaries) provides the most definitive treatment by eliminating the hormonal drive for disease, but residual implants can still persist and cause symptoms, particularly if deep infiltrating lesions were not fully excised. Ongoing research into the immunological and genetic mechanisms of endometriosis aims to develop disease-modifying treatments.

faq.question: What is the difference between endometriosis and adenomyosis?
faq.answer: Endometriosis and adenomyosis are related but distinct conditions. In endometriosis, endometrial-like tissue grows outside the uterus on pelvic organs and the peritoneum. In adenomyosis, endometrial glands and stroma are present within the muscular wall of the uterus (myometrium), causing the uterus to enlarge and become boggy. Both conditions cause dysmenorrhea and heavy menstrual bleeding, but adenomyosis more commonly presents with an enlarged, tender uterus and heavy periods, while endometriosis more commonly causes deep dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain, and infertility. The two conditions frequently coexist — approximately 20-35% of women with endometriosis also have adenomyosis.

faq.question: How is endometriosis managed during pregnancy?
faq.answer: Pregnancy is associated with temporary suppression of endometriosis due to elevated progesterone levels, which inhibit endometriotic implant activity and can cause decidualization or regression of lesions. Many women report symptom improvement during pregnancy. However, endometriosis increases the risk of obstetric complications including miscarriage, preterm birth, placenta praevia, and cesarean delivery. Endometriomas may grow during early pregnancy due to elevated estrogen, and rarely rupture. Women with endometriosis planning pregnancy should be counseled about these risks. Hormonal treatments for endometriosis are contraindicated during pregnancy and must be stopped before conception.

faq.question: Does endometriosis increase the risk of cancer?
faq.answer: Endometriosis is associated with a small but increased risk of certain cancers, primarily endometriosis-associated ovarian cancers (EAOC), particularly clear cell and endometrioid subtypes of ovarian cancer. The absolute risk is low — lifetime risk of ovarian cancer in women with endometriosis is approximately 1-2% compared to 0.5-1% in the general population. The risk is highest in women with large ovarian endometriomas and long-standing disease. Endometriosis is not considered a pre-malignant condition, but regular ultrasound surveillance of endometriomas is recommended. There is no significantly increased risk of endometrial or cervical cancer.

faq.question: Can endometriosis affect the bowel and bladder?
faq.answer: Yes. Bowel endometriosis affects approximately 5-12% of women with endometriosis, most commonly involving the rectosigmoid colon, appendix, and small intestine. Symptoms include cyclical rectal bleeding, painful defecation (dyschezia), bloating, constipation, and diarrhea — often worse during menstruation. Bladder endometriosis (affecting the bladder detrusor muscle) occurs in 1-2% of cases, causing cyclical urinary urgency, frequency, dysuria, and hematuria. Ureteral involvement can cause silent hydronephrosis and renal damage. Diagnosis requires expert imaging (MRI, rectal endoscopic ultrasound). Surgical treatment is complex and requires multidisciplinary teams.

faq.question: How does endometriosis affect mental health and quality of life?
faq.answer: Endometriosis has a profound impact on mental health and quality of life. Women with endometriosis have significantly higher rates of depression (up to 86%) and anxiety (up to 87%) compared to the general population. Chronic pain, fatigue, sexual dysfunction, fertility concerns, and the long diagnostic delay contribute to psychological distress. Work productivity and social participation are frequently impaired — studies show women with endometriosis lose an average of 11 hours of work per week due to symptoms. Comprehensive management should include psychological support, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), pain psychology, and peer support groups alongside medical and surgical treatment.

faq.question: What lifestyle changes help manage endometriosis?
faq.answer: While lifestyle changes cannot cure endometriosis, they can help manage symptoms and improve quality of life. Evidence-based strategies include: regular aerobic exercise (reduces prostaglandin production, lowers circulating estrogen, and improves pain tolerance); an anti-inflammatory diet rich in omega-3 fatty acids (oily fish, flaxseed), fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, with reduced red meat, trans fats, and refined carbohydrates; adequate sleep and stress management (chronic stress worsens pain perception and inflammation); pelvic floor physiotherapy (addresses pelvic muscle dysfunction contributing to pain); heat therapy for dysmenorrhea; and avoidance of endocrine-disrupting chemicals (dioxins, BPA) where possible. Omega-3 supplementation and a low-FODMAP diet may help women with bowel symptoms.

faq.question: Is endometriosis hereditary?
faq.answer: Yes, endometriosis has a strong genetic component. Women with a first-degree relative (mother, sister) with endometriosis have a 7-10 times higher lifetime risk of developing the condition compared to the general population. Twin studies show higher concordance in identical than fraternal twins. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified multiple genetic loci associated with endometriosis risk, including genes involved in hormone signaling, inflammation, and cell adhesion. However, like PCOS, endometriosis is polygenic and influenced by environmental factors. Genetic testing is not currently available or recommended clinically for endometriosis.
